Wilhelm’s description of Mercurius is both accurate and inaccurate. Wilhelm is right in saying that Mercurius is very old, but the diseases that Mercurius is suffering from are not ones that animals suffer from. Usually, those types of diseases would affect an animal both physically and mentally, perhaps even leading them to their death. But the diseases that Mercurius is suffering from originate precisely from the fact that he can not be affected physically int he way of death, that no one below him can end him and this foreknowledge, and that none of these repeats ever lead him to his death. So many years of living this endless wandering life, but not a single endless death to accompany that life. That kind of life, an eternal life of repetition with no death, that is what is inflicting despair and madness upon Mercurius. Those are the diseases that have formed over Mercurius’s very long life, diseases that are mentally eroding his consciousness, forming him into a Maddened God full of despair.

It’s as Wilhelm stated, Mercurius’s head isn’t working properly which was shown through the final fight that explored his paradoxical nature, this eternal life has taken a toll on his intuition and thoughts, and his basic instincts whether it be sleep, eating, or whatever have been hindered/clouded due to his foreknowledge which takes away all the feeling and new/unknown nature that comes with many of the experiences in one’s life, even going as far as to being abel to predict what dreams he will experience, not to mention Mercurius doesn’t even speak in the more natural way that most people do, instead opting to speak in a Jester ambiguous type manner. Wilhelm is both right and wrong in saying that Mercurius is like an animal waiting for natural selection to take him. Yes, Mercurius is waiting for his death to come, but it won’t happen naturally by him being some inferior or damaged being or anything like that. No. He won’t die that way, so he has to forcefully cause his death with his script. That is what Mercurius is waiting for. He is waiting for the day his script will finally cause the death he has yearned for.

At the very end of Interview with Kaziklu Bey, there is a scene of Mercurius in the singularity. The last shot in this scene contains Claudia’s words over a shot of the beach in the singularity. Her words are, “No matter how different our circumstances, we are all heading for the same destination. You wish to arrive in a better place – your sanctuary. Correct?” Claudia’s first sentence is saying that despite how different the circumstances are of each person in the world, including God himself (Mercurius), they are all heading in the same direction being the new world. That is what Mercurius is trying to make his script lead into.

The new world that will be ruled by the Goddess Marie is the direction that everyone is heading into. Unlike before, where everyone was headed in the same direction of Mercurius’s eternal recurrence, now Mercurius is trying to make everyone lead in the same direction of Mercurius’s eternal recurrence, now Mercurius is trying to make everyone head in the direction of Marie’s world.

However, whether Claudia is aware of it or not, that is not Mercurius’s sanctuary. That better world is not the world that Mercurius wishes to be in. No, his desire is clearly stated. His “better place” is death. That is his sanctuary. The script of his will not only leads everyone to the same destination being the Goddess world, but also him to his own death, his own better world.

Yet, Claudia isn’t wrong when she says that they are heading in the same direction as they are. Either Mercurius succeeds at helping Marie create the new world or he repeats it all again, but the better place or the sanctuary that she is referring to is not that new world for Mercurius. In the Marie route, he has to live there, and it does become a better place for him compared to the old world of foreknowledge, but Mercurius’s main yearning that he wants to sate with his script is his death, to finally free him from his despairful life that he has lived, because even death would be a better place than his life. Claudia’s sanctuary was to be an angel of beautiful light, hence why her creation figment became that. But while Claudia may have died as an angel in Wilhelm’s arms, Mercurius just wants to find freedom from foreknowledge in death.

It is there that Mercurius forms the cross in his hand, the same cross that Claudia used as someone who followed God, and then drops it in the sand. The cross obviously ties into God and one’s faith in God, especially since, in this case, that cross was last used by someone who had earnestly believed in God. But in this world, that God is Mercurius. So what does dropping the cross in the sand symbolize?
“Sand is associated with loneliness and is symbolic of the passing of time.”

Dropping the cross that is associated with God in the sand, sand that is associated with loneliness and the passing of time, symbolizes how alone Mercurius has been throughout the eons upon eons that he has lived, and symbolizes just the massive amount of time that has passed for him in this life as God that he has lived. Sand has also been associated with freedom in the past, and considering that the dialogue that is depicted over the shot of the cross in the sand is talking about how Mercurius is heading to his better place, that better place being his death, then perhaps this shot of the cross in the sand also symbolizes hos Mercurius is trying his hardest to free himself from this life that consist of eternal repetition and passing time.
More on Mercurius’s Paradoxical Nature

“Time paradox of elementary particles. It was the very embodiment of a power that could annihilate the contradiction of multiple cosmos occupying a single space. In short, it was a universe-scale suppressor of contradictory phenomena and, as such, could exhibit an unrivaled effect against his cancerous apoptosis.”

The irony behind Mercurius using a power that suppresses and annihilates contradictions is that he is the most contradictory one of all. A walking contradiction using a power that annihilates/suppresses contradictions. His contradictory nature reaches to insane level.

His own powers are part of his contradictory existence. A universe-scale suppressor of contradictory phenomena, but the one who is using that power is the literal embodiment of contradictions, even on a universal scale.

Mercurius made the eternal recurrence law that affected the entire universe, yet despises and wants to destroy it, but he also clings onto his life, resetting the universe once more, not to mention the scripts he has made to cause his death, which he yearns for, just so that he can cling to life via his repetition of the universe, just the same repetition of the universe that continues to torment him with knowledge, drive him deeper into despair and fuel his yearning for death, just for Mercurius to repeat the universe again. Not to mention how Mercurius is stated to be the embodiment of his universal law, the eternal recurrence, meaning that these contradictions that tie into this universal law are being created by the embodiment of this universal law, perhaps even that is now another contradiction formed.

With all of this in mind, this is a universal-scaled contradictory God who uses a power to suppress universal contradictions, yet another contradiction. One can go a step further and say that since he’s using this power to cling to life against the entity he made to fulfill his desire for self-destruction, then that is just another contradiction that is built off the former one. In a way, it’s a rabbit hole. The deeper one looks into Mercurius’s character, the more contradictions one discovers, which further shows that Mercurius truly is the “living antinomy” that Dies Irae describes him to be (yet he’s also stated to have a rigid sense of order, adding yet another layer to the paradox of his existence)

“The two pillars returned his worlds with dignity, as the very cosmos around them melted like a sugar cube in the summer heat. For it was the serpent who had been the most contradictory of them all. It was he who should have suffered the most from the earlier attack.”

This fight also explicitly acknowledges that it is Mercurius who is the most contradictory one of all and that he should have suffered the most from his universal scale suppressor of contradictions attack. This further affirms the interpretations here because him using the power that annihilates/suppresses contradictions when he is the most contradictory one of all is yet another contradiction.
Mercurius’s Dynamic with Ren through Lotus’s Final Words

“‘You are sane’…and uttered those words. Curtly, and with emphasis, ‘We all live in the real world. And while life gives us plenty to cherish, it offers its fair share of misfortune just the same; we march on, hungering after dreams we keep locked up in our hearts, forever unfulfilled.’ The transience of the here and now, that fleeting moment I so adored I would long to make its miracle eternal. A childish notion, true, but one I could not discard; rather, knowing it was a dream never to be fulfilled my thirst for it refused to ever fade. And so we lived, ever discontent, haunted by doughnuts, frail on our feet..’But isn’t that exactly what makes us human?’ I was content to be such a man. ‘Our lives are but petals in the wind; moments lost in the annals of time. No matter how fiercely we struggle to make it outs, eternity will always elude us.”

These are Lotus’s words to Reinhard about the desires within him, the thirst within him, words that ultimately keep Reinhard grounded in being a man striving to be human rather than the beast that he became due to Mercurius. Humans will continue to thirst for things, to yearn for things that are out of their reach, but it is that journey through a life where eternity alludes us and yet we continue marching forward anyway, living our lives to the fullest, that allows us to be truly human, that allows us to live a life where we are content with our existence. Mercurius is the perfect example of someone who became the antithesis to Lotus’s words. Lotus’s words about life containing plenty of things to cherish and plenty of misfortune are true, but by participating in eternal recurrence, Mercurius turned his life into one where he had nothing to cherish and only had misfortune, the only exception being Marie who he had cherished. Mercurius’s eternal recurrence is the perfect example of an impossible dream turned into the possible, of an entity who achieved eternity.

Lotus is aware that the dream he yearns for is one that is impossible, one that can never be fulfilled, and so he keeps it locked in his heart, but that doesn’t mean his thirst for it fades away. No, all it means is that he lives in the finite, limited life he has to the fullest, that he makes the most of his limited life.

However, in the past, Mercurius made his impossible dream come true, the dream of knowing all, the craving of eternal recurrence to achieve that, into something that was possible. Mercurius was able to achieve eternity, and it ruined him. The eternity of loops that he had constantly repeated for an infinity had turned him into someone who had fallen into a pit of despair where he had viewed his life as meaningless, worthless. Mercurius was stuck in that despair, incapable of living his life to the fullest, only yearning so intensely for death itself to take him. Unlike Lotus, who was content with his existence as this man who was both cherished and had discontent, Mercurius was not content to be the man he was, to be such an existence. All he wanted was his existence to end, for it to finally be over.

Mercurius was discontent not because of him being incapable of achieving his impossible dream like Lotus, but because of him achieving that dream and losing himself in the eternity of the eternal recurrence. According to Lotus, eternity alluding us, these dreams that one keeps locked up in their heart and hungers for, the incapability of achieving that dream, all of this is apart of being human, and Mercurius proved Lotus’s words true considering that it was Mercurius being the antithesis to all of this that led to him being inhumane, a lack of humanity within him, visually/physically represented through his lack of a true human body.

These were the consequences that came with reaching eternity, with reaching infinity, and that is why it is important that eternity continues to allude us humans, that death continues to exist for us humans, because as Mercurius and Lotus show, it is that allusion of eternity, that death that allows us to be human, and allows us to meaningfully live out our lives, living them to the fullest. This is what allows us to both cherish the good and experience the misfortune as something new and fresh, something that even Mercurius couldn’t do due to eternity. Eternity, infinity, a life with no death, all it does is destroy the potential one’s life has for happiness, all it does is destroy the potential ones life has to experience a life that Ren describes above, a life of a human, and all one has left with them is the life that Mercurius experienced, the life of a maddened creature who will never be able to recover

“Live your life to its fullest, with your head held high. Indeed, your words do ring true. Man must hunger and lust and crave for as long as his heart beats in his chest. No matter where life takes h im, no matter what nourishment fate offers him, his thirst fades not. But that is fine, merely natural. If there existed any being who refused to accept this sentiment…all that would await him is ruination.”
“If there really was anyone like that, I think his very birth would be an error of nature.”

Both mercurius and Reinhard refused to accept this sentiment and had fallen into ruination. Reinhard didn’t accept his thirst for something to spark within his chest as something that was merely natural. Instead, he became the worst of all things in order to sate that thirst. Reinhard didn’t accept his thirst as a natural thing that humans went through, and that helped lead him to becoming the Beast. Similarly, Mercurius did the same with his boundless thirst for knowledge. He had such a large thirst for knowledge that he refused to accept as something merely natural. Instead he went on to become the God of Eternal Recurrence, creating a world where everything was known to him so that he could sate that thirst. Both Mercurius and Reinhard decided not to live their lives to the fullest as humans or whatever Mercurius used to be, so all that awaited them was ruination. Lotus told Reinhard that anyone like that would have to be an error of nature, and this applies to both. Reinhard was born as the embodiment of Mercurius’s yearning for self-destruction. As Mercurius put it, Reinhard was a cancer cell in the world. Mercurius was born with foreknowledge in the womb (assuming he even had regular parents) and never truly had a human body, was born a natural paradox.

“Death is the inevitable fate of all that lives. I am no exception. And so shall I vow to live and die as a man…as a soldier out of many who merely carries out his sworn duty. I closed my book as if to answer that thought. The story had come to an end, and I had to return to reality. No matter what color the world turned, this was where I was born and where I should and would live. A man must never forget that: should we do so, we will be haunted by our dreams forever, longing after eternity.”

The last couple lines from Lotus here are directly reflected through both Reinhard and Mercurius. For Mercurius, he had forgotten about the inevitability of death and had instead allowed both his dreams of knowing everything and his dream of his ideal death to haunt him. Mercurius theorized that he had initially desired to know everything, which led him to longing after eternity, hence the start of the eternities all those years ago. But as those eternities passed, Mercurius’s dream became to experience his ideal death, and so he had continued to long after eternity, repeating it again and again, refusing to overcome his craving until he achieved his dream death. Those dreams turned Mercurius into a maddened god who lived in despair. He was haunted in this way.
“He was Ahasver, the Wandering Jew - he of many names, and of a life spanning eons.”

In the Kasumi route, Mercurius is referred to as Ahasver, the name given to the Wandering Jew during the 1600s. The tale of the Wandering Jew is about a man who mocked Jesus on his way to the crucifixion and in return, the man was cursed with immortality, to walk/wander the planet forever until Jesus’s second coming. Along the lines of, “I stand and rest, but you will go on, I go, and you will wait till I return,” was what Jesus told the Wandering Jew on that day. Mercurius being referred to as the Wandering Jew symbolizes how he’s been cursed with immortality, how he has repeated this life for eternity upon eternity, how he has wandered this Earth for so many repetitive years of his life. Just like how the Wandering Jew was given many names from “Cartaphilius” to “Buttadeus” to “Issac Laquedem”, Mercurius had also given himself many names as he wandered throughout the eons of his life, from “Nostradamus” to “Karl Ernst Kraftt” to “Alessandro di Cagliostro.” However, the difference between the two stands in the curse received. The wandering jew was cursed with immortality for mocking jesus, the son of God, but Mercurius was cursed by God, himself. Mercurius cursed himself with his own craving of eternal recurrence. The “second coming” mentioned refers to Marie’s becoming the Goddess who will end Mercurius’s suffering.

There is an alternate interpretation that it was Mercurius’s killing of Satanael that turned him into the wandering jew, mocking god and being cursed with immortality, and only in the second coming of God, through Marie, can he be freed.

This actually goes deeper because even the title of Ahasver is but a singular identity used to describe Mercurius and can’t accurately depict the formless void that exists as his “true” self. It but an illusory title to attempt to explain/define Mercurius, but ultimately not being able to grasp his existence properly.

In Mercurius’s conclusion, he talks about how when he was young, he had killed his entire family. Now, the reason why he had done this isn’t made clear and is left ambiguous, but perhaps it was because of his foreknowledge? Keep in mind that Mercurius was cursed with foreknowledge ever since he was in his mother’s womb. He had had it ever since the very beginning of his miserable life which he had repeated so many times, and in Interview with Kaziklu Bey, Mercurius explicitly talked about how he tried so many things, tried to cause change that would allow him to experience something new, fresh, unknown, but that no matter what he did, the foreknowledge was still there tormenting him. Mercurius talked about how if there was anything that could possibly lead him to experience something new, he would do it all. Perhaps Mercurius’s murder of his family was one of his first attempts, if not his first attempt at doing something drastic. The first sin. After all, he was cursed with foreknowledge and torment, dissatisfaction, possibly led him to that event.

One can also interpret Mercurius’s words in his conclusion to be metaphorical for his very beginnings as Lament. The womb is the metaphor for Nerose’s system, and Mercurius killing his family is the metaphor for Mercurius killing Nerose. However, considering that Mercurius himself explicitly talks about how he doesn’t remember how it all began, it’s possible that it’s literal.

Another possible interpretation is that Mercurius might not even be talking about himself truly but about his shades and one of his shades and the memories there. The shades exist as his attempts at becoming an individual and a real person, having a purpose, so it’s possible that due to how formless and ever-decaying he and his mind are, he could have mixed up his memories and the memories of his shades. It’s not made too explicit but yeah.

You could also interpret it as Mercurius telling the truth but also not really. Lament was a person in the 3rd heaven who had his mind ravaged by some cosmic entity, this entity possibly being Mercurius. This would allow Mercurius to have been both always a God and have a real family that he could have likely killed.

Nerose and Mercurius’s plays are interesting because they lead to juxtaposing results. “The future can be changed by the tiniest details. Up to this point, it’s all according to the plot. At least until the actors are ready, it’ll go on without a hitch.” As shown by Nerose’s many statements regarding the story of Paradise Lost, he views Paradise Lost as his own storyline, as his own play that he is creating/directing, similar to how Mercurius views the story of Dies Irae. Both of them lead to their ideal deaths with Nerose’s ideal death being at the hands of Astaroth and Mercurius’s at Marie’s. However, they both function differently. Nerose’s ideal death is so that he dies as a human and becomes a God while Mercurius wants to die as a God and descend into the void, to the unknown.
